1.title: From Rome to the Medieval Boom
1.html:
• The origins of Alsatian viticulture are uncertain, but go back to the Roman conquest — the cultivation techniques may have come from the Narbonnaise region
  • Germanic invasions in the 5th century caused a decline in the vineyards, but they quickly recovered under the impetus of bishoprics, monasteries and the Church
  • 962–1648: Alsace belonged to the Holy Roman Empire and viticulture kept expanding, peaking in the 15th–16th centuries — many wine villages still preserve Renaissance-style buildings from that prosperous era
  • 1481: exports exceeded 600,000 litres, and Alsace wine was sold across northern Europe
  • Thirty Years' War (1618–1648): war, pillage, famine and plague dealt a devastating blow to the vineyards and the economy
2.title: 1871–1945: Turbulent Years of Changing Hands
2.html:
1871: After the Franco-Prussian War, Alsace was annexed by Germany. Production then leaned towards volume, chaptalisation (gallisation) and watering became widespread, and quality and reputation declined.
1871–1918: Overproduction, rising beer consumption that cost export markets, competition from southern wines arriving by rail, and phylloxera and fungal diseases — blow after blow.
1918: At the end of the First World War Alsace returned to France, but the vineyards were nearly abandoned — average yields between 1901 and 1908 were only about 6 hl/ha, and in 1942 hybrid varieties still made up 33% of plantings.
1940–1945: Annexed again by Nazi Germany during the Second World War, then liberated in 1945 and returned to France.

💡 It was the collective will of post-war growers to "choose to become producers of quality white wine" that transformed Alsace into one of France's most important white wine regions.
3.title: After 1945: Building the Modern Quality Framework
3.html:
Within a few decades after the war, a series of regulations built today's Alsace quality system:

1945 — Provisional decree on Alsace wines
1962 — Official AOC status granted
1963 — CIVA (Alsace Wine Interprofessional Council) founded
1972 — All Alsace wines must be bottled in the region of origin
1975 — Decree formally creating the Alsace Grand Cru classification
1983 — First 25 Grand Cru sites delimited
1984 — VT (Vendanges Tardives) and SGN (Sélection de Grains Nobles) sweet wine categories officially named
1992 — A further 25 Grand Cru delimited, bringing the total to 50
2007 — The 51st Grand Cru, "Kaefferkopf", delimited — also the only Grand Cru that allowed blends from the very beginning
4.question: During German rule of Alsace (1871–1918), what was the situation of the Alsace wine industry?
4.options.0: Known for a high-quality, low-yield boutique approach
4.options.1: Leaning towards volume, hit by overproduction and outside competition, with quality and reputation declining
4.options.2: Vineyards were entirely replanted with hops
4.explanation: After 1871 Alsace was annexed by Germany. During German rule the industry leaned towards volume, and overproduction, rising beer consumption, southern wines arriving by rail, and the impact of phylloxera and fungal diseases led to a clear decline in quality and reputation.
5.keyPoints.0: Viticulture dates back to Roman times and flourished in the Middle Ages through the Church (bishoprics, monasteries)
5.keyPoints.1: 1871–1945: German rule, return to France after WWI, annexation again in WWII, liberation in 1945 — four changes of hands deeply shaped the region's character
5.keyPoints.2: The collective will of post-war growers took Alsace from neglect to quality white wine region
5.keyPoints.3: Key dates: 1962 AOC, 1963 CIVA founded, 1975 Grand Cru decree, 1984 VT/SGN named, 1983+1992 total 50 Grand Cru, 2007 the 51st (Kaefferkopf)
